item.title: Artifact 1: Power Supply Rail Splitter & 3-Stage Ripple Decoupling Network
item.description:
The Problem

In precision analog optical receivers, noise on the DC power rails couples directly into high-gain operational amplifier stages and corrupts microvolt-level sensor signals. For this EC EN 340 milestone, our circuit was powered by a single $3.3\text{V}$ DC voltage source (V1) contaminated with a $30\text{mV}$ AC ripple at $1481\text{Hz}$—sitting right inside our target $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ signal passband. Furthermore, the dual-rail operational amplifiers required clean, symmetric $+1.65\text{V}$ (vp) and $-1.65\text{V}$ (vn) supply rails while strictly preserving the starter netlist’s V1, I1, and R1 components.

item.title: Artifact 2: Dual Op-Amp Cascaded Bandpass Noise Filter (1.25 kHz – 3.67 kHz)
item.description:
The Problem

This EC EN 340 design challenge required isolating an ultra-weak $1\text{pA}$ ($2000\text{Hz}$) optical signal (Is) from severe multi-source interference using at most two operational amplifiers. Specifically, the photodiode sensing node (in) was simultaneously driven by:

  • A $1\text{mA}$ DC ambient light offset (In1),
  • A $400\text{nA}$ low-frequency interference source at $100\text{Hz}$ (In2),
  • A $400\text{nA}$ high-frequency interference source at $20\text{kHz}$ (In3), and
  • A $1481\text{Hz}$ power-supply ripple source (V1).

Because the interfering currents were $400{,}000\times$ to $10^9\times$ larger than the $1\text{pA}$ target current, the circuit had to provide massive in-band amplification across the target $1250\text{Hz}$ to $3666\text{Hz}$ frequency window while aggressively rejecting all out-of-band frequencies.

item.title: Artifact 3: Single-Supply Light-Following Robot Filter & Virtual Ground Biasing
item.description:
The Problem

The objective of this EC EN 340 circuit was to condition the optical sensor signal for an autonomous light-following robot. In a mobile robotics platform, only a single $9\text{V}$ battery (V1 = 9V) and $0\text{V}$ ground are available—there is no negative voltage supply rail. Furthermore, static ambient room lighting creates a large DC photodiode offset, while the robot needs to track a modulated $1\text{kHz}$ target light beacon (I1 = 0.1 mA). Without proper DC blocking and mid-rail biasing, the negative half-cycle of the AC signal immediately clips against the $0\text{V}$ ground rail.

item.title: Artifact 4: NGspice Netlist Verification, Capacitor Grounding Audit & Multi-Pole Revision
item.description:
The Problem

When translating complex multi-stage schematics into text-based NGspice netlists in EC EN 340, small node-numbering or grounding errors can silently kill an entire signal chain without throwing a syntax error. Specifically, in our optical receiver simulation, we were required to strictly preserve the starter netlist’s V1, I1, and R1 components and interconnections while integrating a rail splitter, two active bandpass op-amps, and six passive RC filter stages. A common failure mode in early drafts was inadvertently grounding series coupling capacitors (C6/C7 and C23/C24) or mis-referencing the op-amp power and virtual ground nodes, which shunted the target AC signal to ground or locked the op-amp rails.

1. Professional Introduction & Target Role

Target Role: Security Infrastructure Engineer / Data Center Hardware & Systems Engineer

I am Landon Wilmott, a Computer Engineering student at Brigham Young University (BYU) with a minor in Cybersecurity. Alongside my engineering coursework, I supervise student employees in IT support and computer lab maintenance, and I hold CompTIA A+, Network+, and Security+ certifications.

I am actively pursuing Security Infrastructure Engineer and Data Center Hardware / Systems Engineering roles where I can combine my hands-on background in hardware maintenance, analog/digital circuit diagnostics, network virtualization, and systems administration to build resilient, high-availability infrastructure.
